faqs.a: Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10^n, where 1 ≤ |a| < 10. It is the standard way to express very large or very small quantities in science, for example the speed of light as 2.99792458 × 10^8 m/s.

E-notation (like 4.526e-4) is how computers and calculators write scientific notation — e-4 means × 10^-4. Engineering notation restricts the exponent to multiples of 3, matching metric prefixes: 452.6 × 10^-6 is 452.6 micrometers if the unit is meters.
faqs.q: What is the difference between e-notation and engineering notation?

faqs.a: Count every digit starting from the first non-zero digit. In 0.0004526 the significant figures are 4, 5, 2, 6 — four of them. Leading zeros are never significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are.
faqs.q: How do I count significant figures?

faqs.a: Yes. Switch to the “Notation to number” mode, enter the mantissa (4.526) and the exponent (−4), and the calculator shows 0.0004526.
faqs.q: Can I convert scientific notation back to a normal number?

faqs.a: For most school and lab work 3–6 significant figures are plenty. Engineering drawings often use 3; scientific constants may need 10 or more.
faqs.q: How many significant figures should I use?

faqs.a: The calculator handles values from about 10^-308 to 10^308 — the full range of JavaScript doubles. Beyond that it reports the number as out of range rather than guessing.
faqs.q: How large or small a number can it convert?

scientific-notation-calculator.formula:
Scientific form:  x = a × 10^n,  where 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and n is an integer.

n = floor(log10(|x|)),   a = x / 10^n

Engineering form: same idea, but n is rounded DOWN to a multiple of 3,
so the number reads naturally with metric prefixes (kilo, milli, micro...).

E-notation: a × 10^n is written as aEn  (example: 4.526e-4).
howTo: Keep the “Number to notation” mode and type any decimal number into the first field.
Choose how many significant figures you want — 6 is a good default.
Read the scientific form, the e-notation form, and the engineering form in the results.
To go the other way, switch to “Notation to number”, enter the mantissa and exponent separately.
The decimal value appears instantly below.
keyFacts: Any non-zero number x can be written as a × 10^n with 1 ≤ |a| < 10 — that is the definition of normalized scientific notation.
The exponent n is simply floor(log10(|x|)): for 0.0004526, log10 ≈ −3.34, so n = −4.
Engineering notation forces the exponent to a multiple of 3, lining up with kilo-, milli- and micro- prefixes.
E-notation (4.526e-4) means exactly the same as 4.526 × 10^-4 — it is just the computer-friendly spelling.
Zero is a special case: it is written as 0 × 10^0.
